checked.found: Augustus died 19 Aug AD 14 and Tiberius, stepson and adopted heir, succeeded.
AD 41, after Caligula's assassination, the Praetorians found Claudius hiding and proclaimed him; he was a scholar.
Proclaimed by the legions in the East in July 69, won the Year of Four Emperors, founded the Flavian dynasty.
Succeeded Vespasian in June 79; reigned about two years; besieged Jerusalem in 70; remembered as popular.
Sole emperor on Marcus Aurelius's death, 17 March 180 (co-emperor from 177).
Born at Leptis Magna in Roman Africa; proclaimed April 193, marched on Rome, defeated Niger and Albinus, founded the Severan dynasty.
Severus died 4 Feb 211 at York; Geta was murdered 26 Dec 211, leaving Caracalla sole emperor. The article's own sole-reign heading says 212, but the accession is 211.
Priest of Elagabal at Emesa, proclaimed by the troops in May 218 aged about 14.
Became emperor in 270 after Claudius Gothicus died; reunified the empire by 274.
Hailed emperor by the army on 20 Nov 284; humble Dalmatian origins; created the Tetrarchy in 293.
Proclaimed augustus by his army at Eboracum (York) on 25 July 306, the day his father Constantius died.

Constantius II, his cousin, died 3 Nov 361, leaving Julian sole emperor (troops had hailed him Augustus in 360). 361 is right for sole rule; the description says sole emperor on his cousin's death. He tried to restore paganism.
Born in Hispania; named Augustus by Gratian on 19 Jan 379 after the Adrianople defeat of 378.
Made emperor by his father Orestes, the general, on 31 Oct 475; deposed 476, conventionally the last western emperor.

Crowned 5 Oct 610 after overthrowing Phocas, so the year is right. But he was born in Cappadocia, and Wikipedia does not call him a general; his father, the Exarch of Africa at Carthage, was the general. 'A general from Carthage' is therefore unsupported.
checked.suggestion: The son of Africa's governor sailed from Carthage, overthrew a tyrant and took Constantinople's throne, then fought Persia and the Arabs.

checked.found: Crowned 25 March 717, born in Syria (Germanikeia), founded the Isaurian/Syrian dynasty; Arab siege of Constantinople began later in 717.

Constantine VI was blinded on 19 Aug 797 and her sole rule dates from then; the article calls it unprecedented and says she was an empress ruling in her own right. She mostly styled herself basilissa, but the description says only 'imperial title', which holds.

Year 867 is right (the Macedonian dynasty ruled 867-1056). But 'longest-lived' is not supported: Wikipedia calls the Palaiologos dynasty (1259-1453) the longest-ruling, and the Macedonian article makes no longevity claim.
checked.suggestion: A peasant-born courtier murdered his patron and took the Byzantine throne, founding a dynasty that led its golden age.

checked.found: Year 976 is right: he became effective ruler and senior emperor when John I Tzimiskes died on 10 Jan 976 (co-emperor since 960). But his great-uncle Basil Lekapenos was de facto ruler until 985, so 'took effective control' is misleading.
checked.suggestion: The future "Bulgar-Slayer" became senior emperor on the death of John Tzimiskes, soon to expand the empire to a medieval peak.

checked.found: Seized Constantinople on 1 April 1081 as a veteran general; his appeal to the West led to the First Crusade.
Year 1259 is right: proclaimed emperor on 1 Jan 1259, most likely without John IV, at Nymphaion (not Nicaea, which Wikipedia does not mention for this event). He retook Constantinople in 1261.
checked.suggestion: A nobleman had himself crowned co-emperor of the Greek exiles in Anatolia, soon to retake Constantinople.

checked.found: Crowned 6 Jan 1449 (at Mystras); last Byzantine emperor; the empire was then little more than Constantinople ringed by the Ottomans.
